name: Gregory of Nazianzus
also_known_as: Gregory the Theologian; Gregory Nazianzen; one of the Cappadocian Fathers
role: Theologian, poet, and briefly bishop of Constantinople; friend of Basil the Great

died.cause: Natural causes after years of ill health

summary: The orator of the Cappadocian Fathers, whose Five Theological Orations (380), preached in Constantinople, gave classic form to the doctrine of the Trinity and earned him the title 'the Theologian' in the Eastern church. A reluctant churchman who loved solitude and literature, he was ordained against his will, attacked by opponents in Constantinople, made bishop there with imperial backing, and forced to resign during the Council of Constantinople in 381.

key_dates.label: Studies at Athens (c. 350–358) with Basil; also meets the future emperor Julian
Ordained priest against his will by his father, bishop of Nazianzus; flees to Basil, then returns and writes his defence (Oration 2)
Consecrated by Basil as bishop of Sasima, a post he never takes up, straining their friendship
Called to Constantinople to lead its small Nicene congregation at the Anastasia chapel
Preaches the Five Theological Orations; installed as bishop of Constantinople by Emperor Theodosius (November)
Presides over the Council of Constantinople after Meletius dies, then resigns amid opposition and gives a farewell oration
Retires to Cappadocia and writes his autobiographical poems, including On His Own Life

accomplishments.text: Defined the doctrine of the Trinity in the Five Theological Orations (380), defending the full divinity of the Son and especially of the Holy Spirit; the Eastern church calls him 'the Theologian' for them.
Argued against Apollinarius that Christ had a full human mind and soul, in the principle that 'what has not been assumed has not been healed'.
Rebuilt the Nicene community in Constantinople from a house chapel, the Anastasia, before the city's churches were handed over to the Nicenes by Theodosius.
Wrote some 17,000 lines of poetry, including the autobiographical On His Own Life, and many letters; he is one of the great Greek stylists of late antiquity.
Compiled with Basil the Philokalia, an anthology of Origen's writings.
Preached on care for the poor and the sick, especially lepers, in his oration On Love for the Poor (Oration 14).
Wrote two bitter invectives against the emperor Julian after his death (Orations 4–5).

original.phrase: What has not been assumed has not been healed

persecuted_others_note: Gregory did not order violence, but his installation as bishop of Constantinople was part of Theodosius's expulsion of the anti-Nicene clergy from the city's churches, and he later asked the authorities to stop the Apollinarians from holding meetings. He also wrote fierce invectives against Julian and against Arian opponents.

persecuted_others.title: Installed in the cathedral after the expulsion of the Homoian clergy
persecuted_others.targets: Bishop Demophilus and the Homoian (anti-Nicene) clergy and congregations of Constantinople
persecuted_others.summary: When Theodosius ordered the Homoian bishop Demophilus to accept the Nicene creed or leave, Demophilus left, and Theodosius led Gregory into the Church of the Holy Apostles under armed guard. Gregory describes the tense scene in On His Own Life.
persecuted_others.outcome: The Homoians lost their churches in Constantinople.

persecuted_others.title: Called for restraints on the Apollinarians
persecuted_others.summary: In a letter to Nectarius, his successor at Constantinople (Letter 202), he complained that the Apollinarians were being allowed to hold assemblies and urged that this be stopped.

persecution_note: In Constantinople Gregory faced violence from opponents, an attempt to replace him with a rival bishop, and a campaign that forced his resignation.

persecution.title: Attack on the Anastasia
persecution.summary: During the Easter vigil, a crowd of his anti-Nicene opponents, reportedly including monks and poor people incited by Homoian clergy, broke into the Anastasia and threw stones; one of his followers was killed or badly hurt, and Gregory was later accused in court of causing the disturbance.

responsible.name: Homoian clergy and their supporters in Constantinople
responsible.role: Incited and took part in the attack

persecution.outcome: He was acquitted, according to his own account.

persecution.title: Attempted replacement by Maximus the Cynic
persecution.summary: Maximus, a philosopher Gregory had befriended, was secretly consecrated bishop of Constantinople by Egyptian bishops sent by Peter of Alexandria, in an attempt to take over the see. The plot failed, but it humiliated Gregory.
persecution.outcome: Maximus was rejected and later condemned by the Council of Constantinople (381).

persecution.title: Forced resignation at the Council of Constantinople
persecution.summary: Egyptian and Macedonian bishops argued that his move from Sasima to Constantinople broke the canon against bishops changing sees, and others resented his policies at the council. He resigned rather than continue the dispute.

responsible.name: Egyptian and Macedonian bishops at the council
responsible.role: Challenged the legality of his appointment

persecution.outcome: He resigned in June 381 and Nectarius was chosen in his place.

excommunication_note: Gregory was never excommunicated or condemned. He resigned his see in 381 under pressure, but no council deposed him, and he is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church.

sources.citation: Gregory Nazianzen, Select Orations and Letters, trans. Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 7. 1894.
Gregory of Nazianzus, Autobiographical Poems, trans. Carolinne White. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996.
John A. McGuckin, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus: An Intellectual Biography. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2001.
Brian E. Daley, Gregory of Nazianzus. London: Routledge, 2006.
